stem: A nurse is changing the transparent dressing on a stable central venous catheter in an adult client. Which technique best reflects current CDC catheter-site care guidance?

options.A: Perform hand hygiene, maintain aseptic technique, prepare the site with greater than 0.5% chlorhexidine with alcohol unless contraindicated, and apply a sterile dressing; clean or sterile gloves are acceptable for the dressing change.
options.B: Use sterile gloves, but omit skin antisepsis when the previous transparent dressing remained intact.
options.C: Use clean technique without aseptic precautions once a central catheter has remained complication-free for several days.
options.D: Use maximal sterile barrier precautions with cap, mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves, and a full-body drape because routine dressing changes should mirror central-line insertion.

rationale: CDC guidance recommends hand hygiene before and after dressing an intravascular catheter and maintenance of aseptic technique during catheter care. For central venous catheter dressing changes, clean skin should be prepared with a greater-than-0.5% chlorhexidine preparation with alcohol unless chlorhexidine is contraindicated, in which case listed alternatives may be used. Either clean or sterile gloves may be worn for dressing changes, and the site should be covered with a sterile gauze or sterile transparent semipermeable dressing. Maximal sterile barrier precautions are recommended for CVC/PICC insertion or guidewire exchange, not every routine dressing change.
educational_objective: Apply CDC central-line dressing-change principles: hand hygiene, aseptic technique, appropriate skin antisepsis, a sterile dressing, and either clean or sterile gloves; distinguish routine maintenance from insertion-level maximal sterile barriers.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Background Information: Strategies for Prevention of Catheter-Related Infections in Adult and Pediatric Patients
source_version_date: CDC page dated 2024-02-28; current guidance page rechecked 2026-08-16
source_locator: Hand Hygiene and Aseptic Technique → Recommendations 1, 2, and 6; Maximal Sterile Barrier Precautions → Recommendation 1; Skin Preparation → Recommendation 2; Catheter Site Dressing Regimens → Recommendation 1.
source_claim_supported: CDC directs hand hygiene before/after catheter dressing and aseptic technique for catheter care; either clean or sterile gloves are acceptable for dressing changes. For central venous catheter dressing changes, greater than 0.5% chlorhexidine with alcohol is recommended unless contraindicated, and the site is covered with a sterile gauze or sterile transparent semipermeable dressing. Maximal sterile barriers are specified for CVC/PICC insertion or guidewire exchange.

blueprint_locator: Appendix A, printed p. 26, Safety and Infection Prevention and Control → Standard Precautions/Transmission-Based Precautions/Surgical Asepsis: apply principles of infection prevention including hand hygiene and aseptic/sterile technique; evaluate whether aseptic technique is performed correctly.

source_original.stem: A nurse is changing the transparent dressing on a stable central venous catheter. Which technique best reflects current CDC guidance for catheter-site care?

options.A: Perform hand hygiene, use aseptic technique and recommended skin antisepsis, then apply a sterile dressing; clean or sterile gloves are acceptable.
options.B: Use sterile gloves, but omit skin antisepsis if the previous transparent dressing remained intact.
options.C: Use clean technique without aseptic precautions once a central catheter has remained complication-free for several days.
options.D: Use maximal sterile barriers with cap, gown, sterile gloves, and full-body drape because routine central-line dressing care should mirror insertion precautions.

source_original.rationale: CDC recommends hand hygiene and aseptic technique when dressing an intravascular catheter. For dressing changes, either clean or sterile gloves are acceptable; maximal sterile barrier precautions are required for central-line insertion, not every routine dressing change. The site is disinfected with the recommended antiseptic and covered with a sterile dressing.
source_original.source_detail: CDC Intravascular Catheter-Related Infection Prevention Strategies — Hand Hygiene/Aseptic Technique and Catheter Site Dressing Regimens: clean or sterile gloves for dressing changes, recommended antisepsis, sterile dressing. Current CDC intravascular-catheter prevention guidance at exact URL; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. correction_summary: Added 'adult' to the stem to avoid pediatric chlorhexidine-guidance ambiguity. Made the correct option precise to CDC's central-line dressing-change antisepsis recommendation and added the mask omitted from the maximal-barrier distractor. Replaced the prior generic blueprint locator with the exact NCSBN 2026 Appendix A infection-prevention section.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Central venous catheter dressing maintenance and infection prevention
audit_findings.source_authority: CDC intravascular-catheter infection-prevention guidance on an official CDC domain.
audit_findings.currentness: CDC page dated February 28, 2024 remains the current guideline presentation and was rechecked 2026-08-16.
audit_findings.exact_locator: Hand Hygiene/Aseptic Technique, Maximal Sterile Barrier Precautions, Skin Preparation, and Catheter Site Dressing Regimens recommendations directly cover every element of the answer.
audit_findings.claim_audit: The chlorhexidine concentration and alcohol qualifier are directly sourced. The adult qualifier avoids the CDC unresolved issue for young infants. No dressing-change interval is introduced.

distractor_audit.A: Uniquely correct; each component is explicitly supported by CDC recommendations.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because central-line dressing changes include recommended skin antisepsis; an intact prior dressing does not eliminate this step.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because aseptic technique is maintained for ongoing catheter care regardless of uncomplicated duration.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because maximal sterile barriers are specified for insertion/guidewire exchange, not routine dressing maintenance.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A matches all maintenance recommendations; D confuses insertion precautions with dressing care.
audit_findings.cueing: All options describe concrete catheter-care techniques; the key requires knowing the distinction between insertion and maintenance precautions.
audit_findings.blueprint: NCSBN 2026 Appendix A, printed p. 26, explicitly includes hand hygiene, aseptic/sterile technique, and evaluation of aseptic technique under Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Adversarial review checked age-related chlorhexidine ambiguity, sterile-barrier scope, and the clean-versus-sterile glove rule; no unresolved conflict remains.
